---
title: "Explicit bounds and variational reductions"
lang: zh-CN
---

::: {#def-spectral-functional .definition name="Scale-invariant spectral functional" date="2026-09-20" export="def-spectral-functional" status="verified"}
For a bounded open planar domain $\Omega$, write
$$
\lambda_1(\Omega)=\inf_{0\ne u\in H^1_0(\Omega)}
\frac{\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2}{\int_\Omega u^2},
\qquad F(\Omega)=|\Omega|\lambda_1(\Omega).
$$
A polygon is identified with the interior of its convex hull, and its sides
mean effective sides: collinear consecutive edges are merged.
:::

::: {#lem-dirichlet-scaling .lemma name="Scaling and domain monotonicity" date="2026-09-20" export="lem-dirichlet-scaling"}
For $s>0$, $\lambda_1(s\Omega)=s^{-2}\lambda_1(\Omega)$ and
$F(s\Omega)=F(\Omega)$. If $\Omega\subset\Omega'$, then
$\lambda_1(\Omega)\geq\lambda_1(\Omega')$.
:::

::: {.proof of="lem-dirichlet-scaling" status="verified"}
Use the Rayleigh definition in @def-spectral-functional.
For $u\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, put $v(x)=u(x/s)$ on $s\Omega$.
This is a bijection onto $C_c^\infty(s\Omega)$, with inverse $u(y)=v(sy)$.
The chain rule and $x=sy$ give
$$
\nabla v(x)=s^{-1}\nabla u(x/s),\qquad
\int_{s\Omega}|\nabla v|^2=\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2,
\qquad \int_{s\Omega}v^2=s^2\int_\Omega u^2.
$$
Since $H^1_0$ is the closure of $C_c^\infty$ in the $H^1$ norm,
these norm identities extend the map and its inverse continuously to the two
$H^1_0$ spaces. Approximation also gives the displayed weak-gradient identity.
The bijection therefore identifies the two Rayleigh infima up to $s^{-2}$.
The same change of variables gives $|s\Omega|=s^2|\Omega|$;
combining the two scaling laws proves $F(s\Omega)=F(\Omega)$.

If $\Omega\subset\Omega'$, the zero extension of a member of
$C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ belongs to $C_c^\infty(\Omega')$ and preserves both
displayed integrals. Approximate an arbitrary $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ by such
functions. Their zero extensions are Cauchy in $H^1(\Omega')$, and their
$L^2$ limit is exactly the zero extension of $u$. Thus the extension belongs
to $H^1_0(\Omega')$ and preserves the two integrals. The admissible Rayleigh
quotients on $\Omega$ form a subset of those on $\Omega'$, proving monotonicity.
:::

::: {#lem-pentagon-polynomial-upper-bound .lemma name="An explicit regular-pentagon upper bound below nineteen" date="2026-09-20" export="lem-pentagon-polynomial-upper-bound"}
Every regular pentagon $R$ satisfies
$$
F(R)< B:=
\frac{66}{7}(5-\sqrt5)\sqrt{5-2\sqrt5}<19<2\pi^2.
$$
:::

::: {.proof of="lem-pentagon-polynomial-upper-bound" status="verified"}
By @lem-dirichlet-scaling take the inradius to be one and the outward
normal of one edge to be $(1,0)$. Set
$t=\tan(\pi/5)=\sqrt{5-2\sqrt5}$, so $|R|=5t$.
The polynomial
$$
p(x,y)=16-20(x^2+y^2)+5(x^2+y^2)^2
-x^5+10x^3y^2-5xy^4
$$
equals $16\prod_{j=0}^4(1-x\cos(2\pi j/5)-y\sin(2\pi j/5))$.
Thus it vanishes on every side, is positive in the interior,
and belongs to $H^1_0(R)$.

The five rotated copies of
$T=\{(x,y):0<x<1,\ -tx<y<tx\}$ partition $R$ up to null sets.
In polar coordinates $p=16-20r^2+5r^4-r^5\cos(5\theta)$.
Both $p^2$ and $|\nabla p|^2$ are invariant under these rotations.
For nonnegative integers $m,n$, direct integration gives
$$
\int_Tx^my^n=
\begin{cases}
0,& n\text{ odd},\\
\displaystyle\frac{2t^{n+1}}{(n+1)(m+n+2)},& n\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
$$
Expanding the two polynomials and using $t^2=5-2\sqrt5$ yields
$$
\int_Tp^2=\frac{20000t}{297},\qquad
\int_T|\nabla p|^2=\frac{8000(5-\sqrt5)t}{63}.
$$
The Rayleigh principle in @def-spectral-functional gives
$$
F(R)\leq 5t\,
\frac{8000(5-\sqrt5)/63}{20000/297}=B.
$$
Equality is impossible. If the Rayleigh quotient of $p$ were the
first eigenvalue, its minimizing property would give
$-\Delta p=\lambda_1(R)p$ weakly in $R$. Since both sides are
polynomials, this would be a polynomial identity. But $p$ has a
nonzero degree-five term, $\Delta p$ has degree at most three,
and $\lambda_1(R)>0$. Hence the first displayed inequality is strict.

Finally $\sqrt5>559/250$, since $559^2<5\cdot250^2$, and
$$
B^2=\frac{4356}{49}(250-110\sqrt5)
<\frac{439956}{1225}<361.
$$
As $\pi>31/10$, also $19<2\pi^2$.
:::
